nameStory: The 'dovekie' gets its name from its gentle, dove-like appearance and small size compared to other seabirds. This little auk was thought to resemble a tiny sea dove by early observers, though it's actually more closely related to puffins than to any true dove.
description: The dovekie is the smallest member of the auk family, a chunky little seabird about the size of a robin but built like a miniature penguin. These Arctic visitors have short, stubby wings perfect for 'flying' underwater as they chase tiny sea creatures. In winter, they're mostly black above and white below, with a compact body that looks almost neckless when they float on the water like little black and white corks.

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Remarkably small for a seabird - only about 8 inches long, smaller than a pigeon. When floating among other seabirds, dovekies look like toys in comparison.

idTips.label: Stubby bill
idTips.description: Very short, pointed black bill that looks almost triangular from the side. Much smaller and more delicate than the chunky bills of other auks.

idTips.label: Whirring flight
idTips.description: Flies with extremely rapid wingbeats that create a distinctive whirring sound. Wings appear almost blurred in motion, like a large bumblebee.

idTips.label: Winter plumage
idTips.description: Clean black back and wings with bright white underparts. White extends up onto the cheeks and throat, giving a crisp, contrasting appearance.

idTips.label: Cork-like floating
idTips.description: Sits very high on the water like a little cork, often in flocks. Dives suddenly with a quick forward flip, disappearing completely underwater.

habitat: Along New England's rocky coastlines and offshore waters during winter storms and migration. Most often seen from headlands like Cape Ann, Provincetown, or Acadia National Park when strong northeast winds blow them close to shore. They prefer deep, cold waters where they can dive for tiny marine creatures.

seasonality.spring: Rare sightings during March and April as birds head back to Arctic breeding grounds. Often mixed in with other migrating seabirds during stormy weather.
seasonality.summer: Essentially absent from New England waters, spending this season breeding on remote Arctic islands thousands of miles north.
seasonality.fall: First arrivals in November during strong storms. Young birds may be more likely to appear close to shore than adults.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for sightings from December through February, especially during nor'easters that push them toward the coast. Look for them riding out storms in protected bays.

funFact: Dovekies are so perfectly adapted to Arctic life that they can drink seawater - special glands above their eyes filter out the salt, which then drips out through their nostrils like tiny tears.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small dark seabirds, but nothing else is quite this tiny. Young alcids like murres or razorbills are much larger, and storm-petrels have longer, more slender wings and a different flight style.
contextualKnowledge: These birds are called 'little auks' in Europe, which better reflects their family relationships. Despite their penguin-like appearance and swimming style, dovekies can actually fly quite well - unlike true penguins.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus, dovekies are unique among auks for their tiny size. Compared to their closest relatives like puffins and murres, dovekies are much smaller and lack the colorful bills or distinctive head patterns. Think of them as the 'hummingbirds' of the auk family - everything scaled down to miniature proportions.
